problem: Source: 'a very pretty face, of that order the French term _minois chiffoné_'. MODERN says 'of the kind the French call a cheeky little face' — it claims to quote the French term but gives an English phrase, and 'cheeky' mistranslates (minois chiffonné = an irregular but piquant, attractive little face). Keep the French term, glossed.
new_text: First, there was Mrs. Eshton and two of her daughters. She had clearly been a handsome woman and was well preserved still. Of her daughters, the eldest, Amy, was rather small—naive and childlike in face and manner, with a pretty figure. Her white muslin dress and blue sash suited her well. The second, Louisa, was taller and more elegant; with a very pretty face, of the kind the French call a minois chiffoné—irregular but piquant. Both sisters were fair as lilies.

problem: Round-1 repair restored 'prosecuting (or persecuting)' but rendered it with dashes, producing a chain of three dashes ('prosecute—or persecute—your tutor too—pasty-faced Mr. Vining') that is hard to parse aloud. Source uses parentheses; restoring them fixes the reading.
new_text: "We did; and Tedo, you know, I helped you prosecute (or persecute) your tutor too—pasty-faced Mr. Vining, 'the parson in the pip' as we called him. He and Miss Wilson took the liberty of falling in love with each other—at least Tedo and I thought so; we caught various tender glances and sighs which we interpreted as tokens of passion, and I assure you the public soon benefited from our discovery. We used it as a lever to hoist those dead weights out of the house. Dear mama, the moment she got wind of it, decided the whole business was immoral. Didn't you, my lady-mother?"

problem: Source: 'finding a way through the ear to the heart, and there waking sensation strangely'. MODERN adds 'deep' ('stirring something strange and deep'), an intensifier not in the source.
new_text: "Now is my chance to slip away," I thought. But the tones that then filled the air stopped me. Mrs. Fairfax had said Mr. Rochester possessed a fine voice, and he did—a mellow, powerful bass into which he poured his own feeling and force, finding a path through the ear to the heart and there stirring feeling strangely. I waited until the last full, resonant vibration had died away—until the tide of talk, briefly checked, had resumed its flow. Then I left my sheltered corner and made my exit by the side door, which was fortunately close. From there a narrow passage led to the hall. Crossing it, I noticed my shoe was loose; I stopped to tie it, kneeling on the mat at the foot of the staircase. I heard the dining room door open; a gentleman came out. Rising quickly, I stood face to face with him: it was Mr. Rochester.
